transcript.text: micrwave keeps tripping the eletric, not every time but like 1 in 3 when i press start, whole kitchen goes off. had to reset the fuse box 4 times today

That pattern, tripping only sometimes and right when you press start, usually points to the microwave itself developing a fault, rather than your wiring. The moment you press start is when it draws a big surge of power, so a weak component often shows up then.

## First, check which switch is tripping

Open the fuse box after it trips and see which switch has flipped down:

• RCD (the wider switch, usually with a "T" or "Test" button): This trips when electricity is leaking to earth. With a microwave, that typically means an internal fault, such as a breaking-down capacitor, magnetron, or moisture/grease inside. This is the most common cause.
• MCB (a narrower switch, labelled with a number like B32): This trips on overload or a short circuit. It could be the microwave drawing too much, or too many things running on that circuit at once (kettle + microwave + toaster is a classic).

## Quick tests

1. Make sure nothing else heavy is on (kettle, dishwasher, washing machine) when you start the microwave. If it stops tripping, it's likely just overload.
2. Try it on a different circuit, like a socket in another room. If it trips there too, the microwave is the problem.
3. Plug something else into the same kitchen socket (e.g. the kettle). If that's fine, it further confirms the microwave.
4. Check the plug and cable for scorch marks, damage, or a loose fit, and don't use an extension lead or adapter.

## Stop using it for now

Repeated tripping means something is wrong, and it'll likely get worse. Also, don't open the microwave up yourself. It contains a high-voltage capacitor that can hold a lethal charge even when unplugged.

## What to do next

• If the microwave is the culprit, replacing it is usually cheaper than repairing it, unless it's a pricey built-in model. Then a repair technician may be worth it.
• If things trip even with the microwave unplugged, or other appliances cause it too, get an electrician to check the circuit.

If you tell me which switch is flipping (and roughly how old the microwave is), I can narrow it down further.
its the switch that does the kitchen sockets that goes down. microwave is about 5 years old, its plugged into an extension lead with the kettle. sometimes theres a loud bang from inside when it trips

The loud bang from inside is the key clue. Combined with the tripping, it almost certainly means a high-voltage part inside the microwave is failing (usually the capacitor, diode, or magnetron). When it shorts out, it makes that bang and pulls enough current to trip the switch instantly.

## What to do

1. Stop using the microwave and unplug it. This kind of fault won't fix itself and can get worse, with a risk of overheating or fire. Don't open it up, as the capacitor inside can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged.
2. Replace it. On a 5-year-old countertop microwave, a repair (parts plus labour) usually costs as much as or more than a new one. If it's an expensive built-in model, a repair quote might be worth getting.

## The extension lead is a separate problem

Even once the microwave is sorted, don't run the kettle and microwave off the same extension lead:

• A kettle draws about 3kW (roughly 13A) on its own, and a microwave pulls about 1.2–1.5kW. Together they exceed what a 13A extension lead is rated for.
• This won't always trip anything, but it can make the lead and plug overheat, which is a fire risk.
• Check the lead and its plug for discolouration, melting, or scorch marks. If you see any, bin it.

Ideally, plug the new microwave and the kettle directly into separate wall sockets.

## When to call an electrician

If a new microwave plugged straight into the wall still trips the kitchen sockets, or the switch trips when the microwave isn't in use, get an electrician to check the circuit.
